setup: FX call, 7 months, $K/S_0 = 1.075$. The strike pass is done: interpolating between $K/S_0 = 1.05$ and $1.10$ gives an implied vol of 9.275% on the 6-month row and 9.65% on the 1-year row. Only the time pass is left.
ask: The weight on the 1-year row in that last pass is closest to:

options.why: Reversed the weights: 7 months is 1 month past the 6-month row but 5 months short of the 1-year row, so the 1-year row gets the small weight.
Measured 7 months from zero instead of from the lower bracket at 6 months: $7/12$ ignores that the grid starts the bracket at 6 months.
Treated the target as midway; the midpoint of 6 and 12 months is 9 months, not 7.

takeaway: Interpolate inside the bracket: the weight is the distance from the lower grid point divided by the bracket width, so 7 months in a 6-to-12 bracket sits close to the 6-month row.

reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
setup: Standardised P/L, $n = 1{,}000$ observations, 99% VaR estimate $q = 2.326$. The bin around $q$ runs from 2.226 to 2.426. The probability of a loss beyond 2.426 is $p = 0.0076$ and the probability of an outcome below 2.226 is 0.9870. Take $f(q)$ as the probability mass inside the bin.
ask: The standard error $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}\,/\,f(q)$ of the VaR estimate is closest to:

options.why: Stopped at the numerator $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n} = 0.00275$ and never divided by $f(q)$.
Left the $n$ out of the square root: $\sqrt{0.0076 \times 0.9924}/0.0054 \approx 16$.
Read the bin mass as 0.054 instead of 0.0054, a decimal slip that makes the answer ten times too small.

takeaway: A tail quantile is estimated imprecisely: a tiny bin mass in the denominator blows the standard error up, here to about 0.5 on a VaR of 2.3.

reading: MR-10: Financial Correlation Modeling – Bottom-Up Approaches
setup: Gaussian default-time copula with correlation $+0.4$. Borrower B has a cumulative default probability of 21.03% by year 3. Borrower Caa has 60.09% by year 5. Each is read at its own horizon.
ask: The probability that B has defaulted by year 3 AND Caa by year 5, against the independence benchmark (the product of the two), is:

options.label: Below the benchmark
options.why: Applied the correlation with the wrong sign. A positive copula correlation makes joint defaults more likely than independence implies.

options.label: Equal to the benchmark
options.why: Independence only holds at zero correlation; with $+0.4$ the joint probability is lifted above the product.

takeaway: Positive correlation lifts the joint default probability above the product of the marginals, but it can never exceed the smaller marginal (21.03% here).

reading: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
setup: Risk-neutral CIR short rate: $dr = k(\theta - r)\,dt + \sigma\sqrt{r}\,dw$, with $r = 3.60\%$, $\theta = 5.00\%$, $k = 0.40$ and $\sigma = 0.05$. The step is one month, $dt = 1/12$.
ask: The annualised basis-point volatility of the short rate at the start of the month is closest to:

options.label: ≈ 4.7 bp
options.why: Took the drift over the month, $0.40 \times 1.4\% / 12 = 4.7$ bp, which is the expected move, not the volatility.

options.label: ≈ 27 bp
options.why: Scaled the annual figure down by $\sqrt{1/12}$ to a monthly volatility; the question asks for the annualised one.

options.label: ≈ 500 bp
options.why: Read $\sigma = 0.05$ as the volatility itself and skipped the $\sqrt{r}$ factor.

takeaway: In CIR the basis-point volatility is $\sigma\sqrt{r}$: at a 3.6% rate the parameter 0.05 means about 95 bp, not 500 bp, and it shrinks as the rate falls.

setup: Backtest of a one-day 99.5% VaR over 252 trading days. The test is two-tailed at 99% (critical value 2.576), using the normal approximation to the binomial. The model records 5 exceptions.

options.label: Accept the model: 5 exceptions is within the band
options.why: Ignored how small the standard deviation is at a 0.5% tail (about 1.1): the band around 1.26 expected exceptions only reaches about 4.1.

options.label: Reject the model: 5 exceptions is too many

takeaway: At a high confidence level the expected count and its spread are tiny, so even a handful of exceptions can sit more than three standard deviations out.

setup: Basel traffic-light test on 250 days of a 99% VaR model that is in fact correct. Today the model is rejected at 5 or more exceptions, which gives a Type I error probability of 10.8%. The Committee moves the cut-off so that only 6 or more exceptions reject it.
ask: The Type I error probability will:

options.label: Rise
options.why: Mixed up the two errors. Accepting more outcomes raises the Type II error (accepting a bad model); the Type I error shrinks with the rejection region.

options.label: Stay at 10.8%
options.why: The rejection region lost the 5-exception outcome, and that outcome has positive probability under the correct model, so the figure must change.

takeaway: Type I error is the probability of rejecting a correct model. Shrinking the rejection region lowers it, at the cost of a higher Type II error.

setup: A 99% VaR model is backtested over 500 days and rejected at 9 or more exceptions. Suppose its true coverage is wrong. If true coverage is 98% (expected 10 exceptions) the chance of at most 8 exceptions is 33.05%. If it is 97% (expected 15 exceptions) that chance is 3.54%.
ask: A bad model is more likely to slip through (Type II error) when its true coverage is:

options.label: 97%, because it is the worse model
options.why: Assumed a worse model passes more often. At 97% the model averages 15 exceptions, far above the cut-off of 9, so it is almost always rejected.

options.label: 98%, because it sits closer to the cut-off
The two are about equal
options.why: The two figures differ by a factor of about nine (33.05% against 3.54%).

takeaway: The nearer a bad model's expected exceptions are to the cut-off, the more often it is accepted, so mild miscalibration is the hard case to catch.

setup: Internal-models capital charge $\max(\text{VaR}_{t-1},\, k \times \text{VaR}_{avg})$. The bank's own 1-day 95% VaR is USD 40,000 for the previous day and USD 22,000 on a 60-day average. The backtest is in the red zone, so $k = 4$. Both VaRs are scaled to 99% and 10 days with $z = 1.65$ and $2.33$ and the square-root-of-time rule (factor about 4.47).

options.label: The scaled previous-day VaR (about USD 179,000)
options.why: Compared 40,000 with 22,000 and picked the larger, forgetting that $k = 4$ lifts the average-VaR term to 88,000 before scaling.

options.label: $k$ times the scaled average VaR (about USD 393,000)
They tie
options.why: Nothing makes the two terms equal: the $k$ term is roughly 2.2 times the other.

takeaway: In the red zone $k = 4$ multiplies the 60-day average, which usually dominates the latest VaR, so the charge is $k \times$ the scaled average.

setup: Two par bonds, each USD 100m, flat 4% curve, 4% annual coupons: one matures in 1 year, the other in 5 years. Principal mapping puts the whole USD 200m at the average maturity of 3 years. Duration mapping instead puts it at the portfolio's Macaulay duration. The 1-year bond has duration 1.0.
ask: Compared with principal mapping, the duration-mapped 95% VaR will be:

options.label: Higher
options.why: Thought coupons add risk beyond the principal-only maturity. Coupons come earlier, which shortens duration and lowers rate risk.

options.label: The same
options.why: Equated duration with maturity, which holds only for zero-coupon bonds.

takeaway: Coupons pull duration below maturity, so duration mapping lands on an earlier vertex and shows a smaller VaR than principal mapping.

setup: Portfolio of USD 200m: USD 100m in a 5-year 5% par bond and USD 100m in a 3-year 3% par bond (annual coupons). The risk table gives a returns VaR of 8.92% at the 4-year vertex (and other values at other vertices).
ask: Under principal mapping, the whole portfolio is mapped to a single zero at which maturity?

options.label: 3 years, the shorter bond
options.why: Mapped to one bond's maturity instead of averaging by principal.

options.label: 5 years, the longer bond
options.why: Took the longest maturity as the conservative vertex; principal mapping uses the weighted average.

takeaway: Principal mapping ignores coupons and puts all principal at its weighted-average maturity: equal principals at 5 and 3 years give 4 years.

setup: Two bonds under duration mapping onto one yield factor. 7-year bond: price 103.0, modified duration 5.80, 300 held. 20-year bond: price 96.0, modified duration 16.50, 500 held. Yield volatility is 50 basis points; ignore specific risk.
ask: The volatility of the portfolio value is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 900
options.why: Left out the 20-year bond: $179{,}220 \times 0.005 \approx 896$.

options.label: ≈ USD 48,600
options.why: Read 50 bp as 5% (0.05) instead of 0.0050.

options.label: ≈ USD 971,000
options.why: Stopped at the dollar duration and never multiplied by the yield volatility.

takeaway: Dollar duration times yield volatility gives the value volatility. The long bond carries about 80% of it.

setup: Short USD 150m face of a 1-year bond with a 6% coupon paid semiannually. Zero rates (semiannual compounding): 3% at 6 months and 4.1% at 12 months. The bond is decomposed into a 6-month and a 12-month zero position (cash flows USD 4.5m and USD 154.5m).
ask: The total present value of the decomposed position is:

options.label: Negative, and larger in size than USD 150m
Positive, and larger than USD 150m
options.why: Priced the bond correctly but ignored that the position is short, so the sign flips.

options.label: Negative, but smaller in size than USD 150m
options.why: Assumed discounting always pushes value below face. The 6% coupon exceeds both zero rates, so the bond prices above par.

takeaway: A coupon above the discount rates puts the price above par, and a short position flips the sign: about $-$USD 152.8m.

setup: A zero-coupon portfolio is benchmarked to an index whose absolute 95% VaR is USD 2.080m. The portfolio's tracking-error VaR against the index is USD 1.09m, about 52% of the index VaR. Variance improvement is $1 - (\text{TE VaR}/\text{VaR}_{index})^2$, like an R-squared.

options.label: Below 50%
options.why: Forgot to square the ratio: $1 - 0.524 = 47.6\%$. Variance scales with the square of the VaR.

options.label: About 50%
options.why: Equated risk of about half with variance of about half; squaring 0.52 leaves only about 27% of the variance.

takeaway: Variance improvement uses the squared ratio: halving the risk removes about three quarters of the variance.

setup: USD 10m fund benchmarked to an index. Fund volatility 10.0%, benchmark volatility 5.0%, active risk (tracking error) 8.0%, all normal. 95% one-tailed multiplier 1.645.
ask: The fund's 95% tracking-error VaR, compared with its own absolute 95% VaR (using the 10.0% volatility), is:

options.label: Larger
options.why: Combined 10% and 5% (or otherwise inflated the volatility); tracking error is the volatility of fund minus benchmark, here 8%, not a sum.

options.label: The same
options.why: Used the fund's own volatility; tracking-error VaR must use the active-return volatility of 8%.

takeaway: Tracking-error VaR is driven by the active-return volatility alone. At 8% against 10% it comes out smaller than the fund's absolute VaR.
